_meta.//: SOURCE OF TRUTH FOR EVERY OTHER LANGUAGE. Every key that exists here must exist in every other file in this directory, with the same placeholders in it - scripts/i18nprobe.ts fails the build otherwise. The English values are also load-bearing in another way: forty browser harnesses select elements by their visible text, so changing a string here is changing a test selector.

tactics.sliderStyleUp: Wider attack: better attack, weaker scrum and breakdown.
tactics.sliderStyleDown: Forward-led: stronger scrum and breakdown, fewer chances out wide.
tactics.sliderTempoUp: Faster: better attack, but players tire faster and the defence is looser.
tactics.sliderTempoDown: Slower: players tire less, but the attack loses a lot of its edge.
tactics.sliderKickingUp: Kick more: your kickers matter more and it helps in bad weather. Attack and breakdown are weaker.
tactics.sliderKickingDown: Kick less: better attack and breakdown, but mistakes happen in your own half.
tactics.sliderAggressionUp: More aggressive: stronger breakdown, but more penalties and yellow cards. A strict referee punishes this more.
tactics.sliderAggressionDown: More disciplined: fewer penalties and cards, weaker breakdown. Best against a strict referee.
tactics.sliderDefLineUp: Faster line speed: better defence and more turnovers, more offside penalties and cards.
tactics.sliderDefLineDown: Slower line speed: fewer penalties, but their attack gets more time.
tactics.sliderDefWidthUp: Wide defence: stops wide attacks, weaker against forwards through the middle.
tactics.sliderDefWidthDown: Narrow defence: stops forward-led attacks, weaker out wide.
tactics.presetAlloutDesc: Wide and fast. For chasing a score.
tactics.presetShutupDesc: Slow the game, keep shape and kick for territory. For protecting a lead.
tactics.presetCornersDesc: Kick for territory and pressure their exits.
tactics.styleBalancedDesc: No fixed style. Adjust each week.
tactics.styleHightempoDesc: Fast pace. Needs a fit squad.
tactics.styleDefensiveDesc: Kick for position and give away few penalties.
tactics.styleOffloadDesc: Offloads in contact. More chances, more errors.
tactics.defSitBackDesc: Deep line. Fewest penalties, most metres conceded.
tactics.defDriftDesc: Slide towards the touchline. Good against wide attacks, weak through the middle.
tactics.defStandardDesc: Even line and speed. No strength, no weakness.
tactics.defManDesc: Narrow, one-on-one. Good against forwards, weak out wide.
tactics.defPressDesc: Fast rush. The strongest defence, and the most offside penalties.
tactics.z22LongDesc: Kick long. Most ground gained, possession lost.
tactics.z22BoxDesc: Box kick and compete for it. The usual choice.
tactics.z22PlayDesc: Run it out of your 22. More chances, more penalties, and you can get pinned.
tactics.zMidTerrDesc: Kick for the corners. Fewer chances, closer to their line.
tactics.zMidBalancedDesc: Kick or run as the play allows.
tactics.zMidHandDesc: Run through the middle. More chances, further from their line.
tactics.zOppDriveDesc: Forwards carry tight to the ruck. Keeps you camped there and the penalty count down.
tactics.zOppSpreadDesc: Move it wide. The most tries, and the most errors.
tactics.zOppPatientDesc: Build phases. Fewer tries and fewer errors than the other two.
tactics.sliderCommitUp: More players at each ruck: safer ball, fewer attackers.
tactics.sliderCommitDown: Fewer players at each ruck: more attackers and faster ball, more turnovers conceded.
tactics.sliderContestUp: Contest their rucks: more turnovers, thinner defence, more penalties.
tactics.sliderContestDown: Leave their rucks: a fuller defensive line, but they get fast ball.

roles.linkDesc: Attack and breakdown up, scrum down.
roles.aerialDesc: Defence and kicking up, attack down.

playbook.lo_frontDesc: Short throw to the front. Rarely lost, rarely leads to a chance.
playbook.lo_middleDesc: Standard throw to the middle. No strength, no weakness.
playbook.lo_backDesc: Long throw to the back. Better attacking ball, but more likely to be stolen.
playbook.lo_dummyDesc: Fake to the front, throw to the back. Hard for them to read, slow for you to master.
playbook.lo_maulDesc: Catch and drive a maul. The strongest attacking lineout, and the slowest ball.
playbook.lo_topDesc: Ball tapped straight down to the 9. Fast ball, but no maul to drive.
playbook.sc_channel1Desc: Ball out quickly past the hooker. Fast ball, less push.
playbook.sc_holdDesc: Hold the ball at the No. 8's feet. A stable platform.
playbook.sc_shoveDesc: Push hard for a penalty. Wins penalties if your pack is stronger, concedes them if it is not.
playbook.sc_wheelDesc: Turn the scrum and attack off the side. Needs a technically strong pack.

armsrace.tapeSet: Their analysts have your {move_k} on {pct}% of your first-phase ball, and this coach sets up to stop what the tape shows.
armsrace.tapeCalm: Their analysts have your {move_k} on {pct}% of your first-phase ball, but this coach does not change much for it.
armsrace.tapeUnread: Their analysts have your {move_k} on {pct}% of your first-phase ball. The report can't say whether they'll set up for it.
armsrace.tapeRetired: Their analysts have your {move_k} on {pct}% of your first-phase ball, but you've dropped that call, so there's nothing for them to set up for.

moves.mv_1331Desc: A pod of three forwards either side of the ruck and a forward on each edge. Carries across the whole width.
moves.mv_242Desc: Four forwards in midfield and two back-rowers out on each edge, running at the backs.
moves.mv_backdoorDesc: Three forwards off the 9 as a pod, with the 10 hidden behind them for the pass out the back.
moves.mv_crashDesc: The 12 runs a hard, straight line off the 10 and takes the contact. Simple, safe, and over the gain line.
moves.mv_switchDesc: The 10 runs across the field and the 13 cuts back behind on a scissors. Wrong-foots a drifting line.
moves.mv_loopDesc: The 10 misses the 12, loops round the back and takes it again outside. Makes an extra man.
moves.mv_decoyDesc: The 12 runs a hard decoy line and the 10 passes out the back of it to the 13 or the 15.
moves.mv_blindDesc: Off the scrum the 8 picks up, the 9 goes blind and the 11 wraps round on the outside.
moves.mv_insideDesc: The 10 drifts across the defence and pops the ball back inside to the 12 on a late line.
moves.mv_strike13Desc: Lineout strike: the 12 takes it flat and the 13 hits a short line through the midfield gap.
moves.mv_winginDesc: The blind wing leaves his touchline and hits the 10-12 channel at pace off a flat 10, with the 12 as the decoy. The man nobody counted.
moves.mv_widthDesc: Short flat passes along the line and the 15 into it from depth, then the ball on to the far touch. Width off first phase.
moves.mv_peelDesc: The maul sets, the hooker takes it off the back and runs across it, and the blind wing cuts in on his shoulder.
moves.mv_maulswitchDesc: Red zone only. The lineout splits into two pods; they compete at one, the ball goes to the other, and it binds and drives for the line.
moves.mv_tapDesc: Penalty slot only. The 9 taps, one pod shapes to drive, and the ball goes to the second pod and round its corner.
moves.mv_tapspreadDesc: Penalty slot only. The 9 taps, the forwards run hard flat lines at the mark, and the ball goes out the back of them to the 10 and along the line.
moves.mv_tapgoDesc: Penalty slot only. The 9 taps and pops to a forward on a hard line off the mark, two more bind on him, and they drive on.
moves.mv_crashswingDesc: Two phases: a flat crash ball with a back-rower on the shoulder, then off the quick ruck the ball goes back the other way to the far edge.
moves.mv_loop9Desc: The 10 runs straight at the fringe and the 9, who followed his pass round the back, takes the tip outside him.
moves.mv_crosskickDesc: A flat line draws them up and the 10 puts the ball on the far wing, running onto it.
moves.mv_grubberDesc: Against a line rushing up, the 10 rolls it through between two defenders for the centres to chase.
moves.heading: Playbook
moves.headingSub: set moves you call and drill
moves.mixLabel: Primary strike on {pct}% of the ball both can run off

bench.split53Desc: 5 forwards and 3 backs. Cover for every position.
bench.split62Desc: 6 forwards and 2 backs. Stronger up front late on; a back injury may put a forward in the backline.
bench.split44Desc: 4 forwards and 4 backs. Fresh legs and cover out wide; less push late on.
bench.briefOrdersDesc: Plays the same job as the player replaced.
bench.briefImpactDesc: More carrying, less defending. Tires quickly.
bench.briefShoreDesc: Tackles and discipline. Fewer risks in attack.
bench.briefManageDesc: Kicks for territory to keep play in their half.

analyst.noReadsYet: No reads followed yet this era.
analyst.followedReads: Followed {n} of his reads: right {right}, wrong {wrong}.
analyst.sureStake: I'd stake my job on this
analyst.sureHunch: It's a hunch, but a decent one
analyst.andTest: , and {name} is the one to test
analyst.weakScrum: their scrum goes backwards under pressure
analyst.weakLineout: their lineout is a lottery beyond the front pod
analyst.weakDefence: their defensive line comes up in ones and twos
analyst.weakAttack: they have no shape once the first phase breaks down
analyst.weakKicking: their kicking game hands territory back every time
analyst.howScrum: Live scrummaging all week. Squeeze them and the penalties come.
analyst.howLineout: Set-piece work: contest their throw and the platform collapses.
analyst.howDefence: Attacking shapes. Move them side to side and holes appear.
analyst.howKicking: Attacking shapes and quick counters off their loose kicks.
analyst.howAttack: Defensive drills. Squeeze the space and let them run out of ideas.
analyst.noMatchToStudy_w: No match this week, so nothing to study. She will have a read on the next opponent as soon as one is in the diary.
analyst.followedReads_w: Followed {n} of her reads: right {right}, wrong {wrong}.

forms.runningSubj: {club} are playing with the handbrake off
forms.running: The ball is going through the hands at {club}. Supporters have started calling it running rugby, and quick backs around the league have noticed.
forms.kickingSubj: {club} are winning it with the boot
forms.kicking: Territory, pressure and a kicking game the rest of the league has learned to expect. Kickers and good decision makers want to play in a side like this.
forms.pack: Set piece, maul, carry, repeat. {club} are becoming a forwards' club, and big forwards across the league are taking an interest.
forms.flair: {club} are going wide early and the outside backs are cashing in. Back-line flair is fast becoming what the club is known for.
forms.academy: More and more of the minutes at {club} are going to players they brought through themselves. Young players are listening and the academy is sending up better classes. The terraces love it, and they will notice if a big cheque ever pushes one of their own out.
forms.spenders: {club} are buying rather than building, and the market knows it. Players who follow the money are ringing first.
forms.prudent: Money in the bank and the books going the right way. Sponsors like it, and so do players who plan a career. The board will expect it to stay that way.
forms.stretched: The balance at {club} is heading the wrong way, and people have started to say so. The board will be watching the accounts closely.

identity.fades: '{label_k}' no longer describes {club} the way it did.
identity.fansObjectSubj: The terraces question a big signing
identity.fansObject: {club} built a name on bringing their own through, and some supporters are unhappy that {player} has arrived for a big fee in the shirt {own} has been wearing. {own} is said to be quietly disappointed.
identity.academyKept: Homegrown regulars at {club} this season: {n}. The supporters see the club keeping its word, and the mood on the terraces is better for it.
identity.academyStalled: {club} are meant to be an academy club, but not one homegrown player held down a place this season. The supporters have noticed, and so has the board.
identity.prudenceBroken: {club} had earned a name for careful money, and this season the balance fell a long way. The board has made it clear that is not what it signed up for.
identity.stretchedMending: After a spell of living beyond their means, {club} have put money back into the account this season. The board has noticed, and is pleased.

philosophy.packBlurb: Forward-led: mauls from lineouts, pick-and-go, pressure at the scrum.
philosophy.packSoft: Weak if you slow their ball down.
philosophy.widthBlurb: Moves the ball wide early and offloads in contact.
philosophy.widthSoft: Weak if you win the collisions and force handling errors.
philosophy.tempoBlurb: Quick taps and fast rucks to tire you out.
philosophy.tempoSoft: Weak if you keep your defensive shape; they tire late on.
philosophy.squeezeBlurb: Kicks for territory and puts pressure on your exits.
philosophy.squeezeSoft: Weak against strong counter-attack from their kicks.
philosophy.blitzBlurb: Fast rush defence and plenty of contestable kicks.
philosophy.blitzSoft: Weak to kicks and passes behind the rush.
philosophy.counterSoft: Weak if you keep the ball through the phases.
philosophy.chaosBlurb: Fast, physical and loose. Strong in broken play.
philosophy.chaosSoft: Weak against a disciplined side: they concede penalties.
philosophy.structureBlurb: Set plays and patient phases. Few penalties conceded.
philosophy.structureSoft: Weak when rushed into unplanned play.
philosophy.counter_pack: Match them up front. Do not go wide off slow ball.
philosophy.counter_width: Kick for territory so they have to attack from deep.
philosophy.counter_squeeze: Run their kicks back at them.
philosophy.counter_blitz: Attack around the rush, not into it, and keep penalties down.
philosophy.counter_counter: Keep the ball. Kick only when your chase is ready.
philosophy.counter_chaos: Stay disciplined and let them give penalties away.
philosophy.counter_structure: Put them under pressure early with line speed.

matchday.optCornerD: Lineout five metres out. Back the maul and go for the try.
matchday.optPostsDLead: {kicker} lines it up. Safe three - levels or leads.
matchday.optTapD: Catch them flat-footed and keep the tempo up.
matchday.partnershipsSub: the more games together, the better they click
matchday.pausedTitle: Play is paused - change the picture
matchday.penCall: Penalty - your call from the touchline
matchday.planAir1: We win the air. Kick for touch and squeeze them for territory.
matchday.planAir2: Their lineout wobbles under pressure. Kick to the corners and go after their throw.
matchday.planApply: Apply the plan - adjust my tactics
matchday.planHeated1: This one could boil over. Be the calmer side and let them lose their heads.
matchday.planHeated2: Bad blood in this fixture. Let them throw the punches and take the points from the penalties.
matchday.planLenient1: {ref} lets it flow - lift the tempo and fight every breakdown.
matchday.planLenient2: {ref} doesn't blow much. The breakdown will be a scrap today, so win it.
matchday.planScrumThem1: Avoid the arm wrestle - their pack is a handful. Play away from the set-piece.
matchday.planScrumThem2: Do not feed their scrum. Quick taps, quick lineouts, keep the big lads honest and blowing.
matchday.planScrumThem3: Their pack wants a fight we cannot win. Deny them the set-piece and stretch the game.
matchday.planScrumUs1: Their scrum creaks. Keep it tight and squeeze the penalties out of them.
matchday.planScrumUs2: We have them at the scrum. March them backwards until the referee gets bored of whistling.
matchday.planScrumUs3: Their front row is the weak link. Every scrum is three points waiting to happen.
matchday.planStrict1: {ref} cards early - discipline first at the ruck.
matchday.planStrict2: {ref} referees the letter of the law. Stay on your feet, hands off, no cheap shots.
matchday.planTired1: Their legs are heavy this week. Run them off their feet.
matchday.planTired2: They backed up a hard match and it shows. High tempo from the first whistle and they will crack late.
matchday.planWet1: {weather} forecast. Put boot to ball and pin them in the corners.
matchday.planWet2: {weather} on the way. Territory wins this one: kick long, chase hard, let them make the mistakes.
matchday.planWet3: Filthy weather due. A day for the boot and the maul, not for throwing it about.
matchday.planWide1: Their edge defence is the soft spot. Go wide and shift the point of attack.
matchday.planWide2: Numbers out wide win this. Two passes past the ruck and they are scrambling.
matchday.planWide3: Their wingers tuck in. Get it to the edge quickly and the tries are there.
matchday.prepAttack: Attacking Shapes - strike moves drilled all week. Attack sharpened.
matchday.prepDefence: Defensive Drills - the wall is built. Defence sharpened.
matchday.prepFitness: Conditioning - the legs will last longer than theirs.
matchday.prepRecovery: Recovery Week - fresh bodies, full tanks.
matchday.prepSetpiece: Set-Piece Work - scrum and lineout honed to a point.
matchday.quote1: We know how they want to play. We're ready for it.
matchday.quote2: No excuses from us this week. We've targeted this one.
matchday.quote3: They're a good side, but this is our patch.
matchday.quote4: People keep writing us off. Suits us fine.
matchday.quote5: We've had a good week. You'll see a response on Saturday.

matchday.wxFxDamp: A greasy ball: expect a few more knock-ons, and the boot and the carry come into it.

matchday.wxFxSnow: Snow on the ground: the ball will be a bar of soap, and tight rugby wins.

matchday.surfFx_hybrid: Grass stitched with fibre: true and firm, whatever the weather.
matchday.surfFx_artificial: Hard and fast underfoot: it drains well, every collision costs a little more, and the home side knows its bounce.

matchday.htWetTight: It is wet: one pass too many is a turnover. Carry it, and use the boot.
matchday.htWind: The wind is taking the long kicks: find touch short and keep it in hand into it.
matchday.htUncontested: The scrums are uncontested now: the set piece is out of it, so play off the lineout.

tacticsScreen.exitBoxDesc: The safest exit, but you give them the ball.
tacticsScreen.exitLongDesc: Kick for field position. Safe and simple.
tacticsScreen.exitCounterDesc: Keep the ball and run. Risky in your own half.
tacticsScreen.exitFifty22Desc: A 50:22 attempt. Big gain if accurate, loses ground if not.
tacticsScreen.penCornerDesc: Kick to the corner and back the maul.
tacticsScreen.penTapDesc: Tap and go, running the play in your Playbook's Penalty slot. Fast, but more errors.

tacticsScreen.the23Sub: the first three cover the front row

tacticsScreen.prepFitnessLong: Players tire about 8% slower next match.
tacticsScreen.prepRecoveryLong: Everyone recovers extra condition this week.

tacticsScreen.withTheBallSub: how you attack with the ball

tacticsScreen.kickTerritoryDesc: Kick to touch for field position. Best if your lineout is stronger.
tacticsScreen.kickContestDesc: High kicks to win the ball back. Good in the wet, gives the ball away in the dry.
tacticsScreen.kickAttackDesc: Grubbers and cross-kicks. Good against a rush defence; loses territory and is poor in the wet.
tacticsScreen.kickBalancedDesc: A mix of kicks. No strength, no weakness.

staff.roleAssistantDesc: Sharper sessions: bigger training gains, faster youth development and better auto-picked sides.
staff.rolePhysioDesc: Shorter injury layoffs and quicker recovery between matches.
staff.roleScoutDesc: Faster, wider scouting knowledge across the leagues.
staff.roleAttackDesc: Shape and strike moves. A sharper attack on match day and bigger gains in attack training.
staff.roleDefenceDesc: Line speed and the system. A meaner defence on match day and bigger gains in defence training.
staff.roleScrumCoachDesc: Scrum and lineout. A tight five that wins you penalties on match day.
staff.roleKickingDesc: Kicking from hand and off the tee. Better territory, and more goals under pressure.
staff.roleAcademyCoachDesc: Runs the second squad. Academy players develop faster under a proper mentor.

report.tut1b: 1. One button moves the game on.
report.tut1: It says {continue} at the top of the screen. Press it and a day goes by. Press it again and again and you walk through the week - who is injured, what the press want, who is for sale - until Saturday, when the button says {matchday}.
report.tut2: Tap the clipboard at the bottom, then {team} - you land on the team sheet. Tap two players to swap them, or press {bestXV} and let your assistant draft one - then change anything you disagree with. You have fifteen starters and eight replacements.
report.tut3: Press {kickOff}. You say a few words to the players first - pick whichever one feels right, there is no wrong answer. During the game you can bring on replacements or change how you play. When you win a penalty near their line, you choose: kick at the posts for three points, or go to the corner and try for a try.
report.tut4: Every number in this game has a page explaining it, in plain English, in {handbook} (bottom right, Manager). It has a search box. If something confuses you, it is in there.
report.tut5: Find out. A lost Saturday is not you doing it wrong - it is the other side turning up. The board tells you what it expects on the Finances screen, and you have a season to deliver it.
report.crashBody: Your save is safe. The game writes to this device every week, so the worst you can lose is what has happened since the last Continue. Going back to the title screen usually clears it, because it is almost always one screen misreading something rather than the save itself.
report.crashNote: Report this attaches that message, the build and the screens you came through - you do not have to copy anything down.

handbook.a1: Everything runs off the button in the top corner. It reads Continue on an ordinary day and Matchday when the match is next. Each press moves the week on a step: through the days, into the match, then the round's results. Anything that happens lands in your inbox on Home. If something needs an answer before the week can move, the button tells you what.
handbook.a10: A pre-match briefing that reads the opponent and suggests a full tactical setup, applied with one tap. A better assistant gives better advice. It is a starting point, not an instruction.
handbook.a11: The one thing that matters most about the next match: win and you go top, the board meets on Monday whatever happens, a man is one try short of fifty, a side you have lost to three times running. It reads the table, the board, the grudges and the milestones and picks the biggest. When there is nothing worth saying, it says nothing.
handbook.a12: A great deal. Each referee has his own tolerance, and some will reach for a card where others talk. A yellow puts you a man down for ten minutes and the scoreboard usually shows it. A red is worse: the player leaves the field, and he picks up a ban of one or more matches afterwards. Aggressive players and the Hot Head trait get carded more.
handbook.a13: Yes, and it is a gamble rather than a free go. The panel reads the player's record: a player with a clean record on a one-match ban wins about two hearings in three, a repeat offender on a long ban almost never does, and most appeals fall somewhere near a coin toss. Win and a match comes off. Lose and a match goes on, and the board notes that you wasted everyone's afternoon.
handbook.a14: Rain and wind both make handling and kicking harder and push games towards the forwards. Snow more so. A wet afternoon is a good week to have picked a big pack and a boot.
handbook.a15: It plays the match out immediately and shows you the full-time score and report, without the tick-by-tick. Useful for a friendly or a week you do not want to sit through. You keep every consequence: injuries, cards, ratings and all.
handbook.a16: You're asked before kick-off. Full commentary is every line as it happens, with live stats, and the pitch shown for tries and the big moments. Big moments skips to the next thing that matters: it stops for scores, cards and injuries but not every ruck, and you still get half-time and the hour mark. Assistant hands the touchline to your assistant and takes you straight to the report. Your choice is remembered for each competition, so you can watch the league and skip the friendlies. During a match, the cog switches between the first two.
handbook.a17: Five and three is the standard 23 and it is neutral: cover everywhere, no extra weapon. Six and two is a bomb squad: once three replacements are on, your scrum, breakdown and defence get stronger and your attacking shape suffers. Four and four is the reverse: width and cover in the backs, less shove. Neither does anything if you leave the bench sitting there.
handbook.a18: Cover. Name six forwards and you only have two backs, so if a centre limps off after both are used, a flanker finishes the game at 13. That costs you in attack and costs you more in defence, and no amount of shove up front gets it back. That is the price of a bomb squad.
handbook.a19: Because players are people. Every man has two things the game never shows as a number: how consistent he is week to week, and what a big occasion does to him. Some turn up every Saturday. Some are capable of anything, good or bad. Some grow an inch walking out for a final or a derby, and some freeze. Favourites feel it too: on the big day the gap between the sides closes a little, which is why cup upsets happen. You learn who is who the way a real coach does, by watching a season of ratings. During a match your assistant reports condition the same way, "blowing", "tiring", "out on his feet", because nobody on a touchline knows a man is at exactly 43%.
handbook.a2: Three things. Check the XV and the bench on the Team tab. Pick a dressing-room talk on the Talk tab: the words you choose really do move morale. Then confirm you are ready. After that, nothing changes until kick-off.
handbook.a20: What you say to a replacement as he pulls his shirt on, set for each bench seat on the Tactics bench page. Do the same job is neutral. Make an impact buys carrying at the cost of defence, and he tires quickly. Calm it down buys tackling and discipline and takes fewer risks in attack. Kill the clock kicks for territory to keep play in their half. Only the first three briefed replacements to come on take effect, so choose who gets one.
handbook.a21: It sets what each player has been told against what the team sheets actually say. Set his role (key player, rotation, squad player, prospect, or not in plans) and the page shows the games he was promised, the games he has had, and how he feels about the gap. A player short of what he was promised gets restless and in the end wants out. An honest role costs you nothing.
handbook.a22: Only for leaving out players you told otherwise, and only those outside this week's matchday 23. Nobody in the 23 has a grievance this week. A frozen-out player settles into a grudge rather than sinking further, so it shows up as transfer requests, knocks on your office door and contract trouble, not as a hidden penalty on the side you pick.
handbook.a23: Four jobs beyond the armband: who leads the pack, who runs the defensive line, who runs the attack, and who sets the standards. A job does not make the side stronger overall. It moves the leadership you already have onto one area and away from the rest, so a defensive leader sharpens the defence and costs you some attacking shape. Only starters with real authority can take one. A strong leader can take two, but each is its own trade-off: a second job pulls more of the side towards his areas, it does not add a bonus.
handbook.a24: Attributes are shown on a 1 to 100 scale and describe what he can do. Current Ability is a single 1 to 100 summary of how good he is now, Potential is how good he could become, and Potential stays hidden until your scouting knowledge of him is good enough. Form is a rolling 1 to 10 on recent performances, morale is how he feels, condition is how fresh he is, and sharpness is how much rugby he has played lately.
handbook.a24_f: Attributes are shown on a 1 to 100 scale and describe what she can do. Current Ability is a single 1 to 100 summary of how good she is now, Potential is how good she could become, and Potential stays hidden until your scouting knowledge of her is good enough. Form is a rolling 1 to 10 on recent performances, morale is how she feels, condition is how fresh she is, and sharpness is how much rugby she has played lately.
handbook.a25: Tap Team to open the team sheet. Best XV asks your assistant for his best side: a good draft that takes form into account, but it is his opinion, not the right answer. To change it, tap a player, then another, and they swap. Tap the same slot twice for the full squad list. How the side plays (roles, set piece, bench shape, prep, game plan) is on the Tactics screen.
handbook.a26: Your assistant names the side once and it stays that way: nobody updates a sheet you never touch for form, fitness or new signings. He is decent, not perfect, and misjudges a man here and there, less often the better his badge. Picking the XV yourself is worth real points over a season, and so is a better assistant if you want to delegate. The press desk is the same: every question you leave unanswered costs a little board confidence and fan mood.
handbook.a27: On the Tactics tab each shirt can be given a role that shapes how he plays: a ball-playing ten, a fetcher at seven, a sweeping full-back. A role suits some players more than others, and it works best on a man whose attributes already point that way.
handbook.a28: Five pairings get better the more they play together: each prop with the hooker, the two locks, the half-backs and the centres. A pairing goes from brand new to settling in, settled, established and finally telepathic, and every step is worth something on the pitch. Rotating those five spots every week costs more than it looks.
handbook.a29: Pair any player aged 20 or under who is still below his potential with a senior pro of 28 or more, on the Mentoring tab of the Team Report. Four pairings at a time, five with a Centre of Excellence at level 3 or better. Choose the young player first and every senior who could take him is listed with how close their positions are, his leadership, his caps and what he could teach. Nobody knows how the two will get on until they try: for the first month the card only says it is too early to tell, and after that it says in plain words how it is going. Character decides most of it: a Leader teaching an Ambitious or Temperamental kid is the best combination in the game, two Temperamentals together the worst, and a Mercenary teaches almost nothing. The same position helps, the same unit (front row, back five, halves, outside backs) a little, and experience a little more. Each week the pairing can coach a point into something the senior is clearly better at and the kid's position needs, paid for from the kid's least needed attributes like all training, and can add a rating point while he is below his potential: about one a season for an average pairing. A senior can take two kids, but each then learns at three-quarter speed, and he will mention it in the eight-week reports. Slowly the kid may also take on his mentor's character, roughly a one in three chance across a season. The Mentoring tab keeps a record of what each kid has gained. A pairing ends itself when there is nothing left to teach (the kid turns 21, reaches his ceiling or takes on his mentor's character), and one that is not working can be ended on its card.
handbook.a3: Yes, at any stoppage. The clipboard button opens tactics and replacements mid-match, so you can shut a game down, chase one, or get a tiring front row off. Eight men sit on the bench and you can use all eight, as the laws allow, front-row cover included. A man who has come off does not come back, except for blood and front-row cover. The game suggests natural cover first rather than putting a winger in the second row.
handbook.a30: Three layers. The whole squad has a weekly emphasis; up to five youngsters can have a development focus for faster growth; and a handful of men can go on personal plans, individual programmes in a chosen area. Your assistant's badge sets how many plans can run at once, the matching specialist coach and the Training Paddock make a plan land more often, and younger men take more from it. A man on a plan does his programme instead of the squad session, not both. Progress is slow. Training decides where ability goes, not how much there is: every point a programme adds is paid for by a point from an area it does not cover, taken from what the position needs least, and it stops near the level the position plays at. A plan also adds one rating point each summer to anyone below their potential.
handbook.a31: Your backroom staff are named people, each Unbadged or holding a Bronze, Silver or Gold badge, and the badge is what they are worth to you. You can send a coach on a course for the next one: sixty thousand pounds for each badge already held, and 58 in every 100 pass. The examiners decide the same day. The fee is spent either way, a pass comes with a pay rise, and a coach who fails cannot sit it again for four weeks.
handbook.a32: Watch condition and minutes. A player who passes 1,300 minutes in a season is in the red zone and starts breaking down. Rotate, use the recovery preparation on short turnarounds, and build the gym: every level of the Strength and Conditioning Gym gives back condition every week.
handbook.a33: A better physio and a better Recovery Centre both shorten layoffs. The Medical Centre screen lists everyone out, with return dates. You can pay for a specialist consult on a bad one, and wrap a man with a long injury record in cotton wool for a week. Head injuries follow the HIA protocol and the length of the layoff is not yours to decide.
handbook.a34: A signature edge, or flaw. The Step beats defenders and scores tries, Siege Gun kicks from anywhere, Jackal wins turnovers, Big-Game Player grows in knockouts and derbies, Hot Head is one flashpoint from a card every week. They show on the player's profile and they change what happens on the pitch.
handbook.a35: Leadership is the attribute that matters, and the Leadership card on the Team screen's Selection tab lists your squad sorted by it. A strong captain lifts attack and defence and keeps tempers in check. Name a vice-captain too: he steps up at half the effect when the skipper is missing, and one day he will take the armband for good.
handbook.a36: In week 2 of every season the office asks how you want to pitch the year against the pundits' predicted finish, and your answer stands until the summer. Aim high and every result is measured against your own words: wins earn about 15 per cent more credit with the board and defeats cost about 30 per cent more. The board also puts extra money behind you, and takes it back off next season's budget, with interest, unless you beat the prediction or win the league. Keep heads down and the board reacts 15 per cent less either way: safer when losing, less credit when winning. Back the board's targets and results are judged as normal. There is no right answer. It is a bet on your own season.
handbook.a37: The page between seasons, and you cannot skip it. Once the last match is played and the summer has been processed, Continue opens the Annual: the year's champions, your silverware if there was any, and confirmation that the season is filed (the Roll of Honour, your Annals on the Manager Legacy screen and the record books are all updated before you see it). One button starts the new season, and nothing moves until you press it.
handbook.a38: The career goal you chose at the end of the New Career wizard: take a Championship club into the top flight, win the league and Europe with one club, build a first team out of your own academy, coach a nation to the World Championship, and a handful more. The options depend on your starting club, so a Premier Division giant is never asked to "reach the top flight" and an English National One side is never asked to "win it all with what you have got". It sits on Home every week with an honest line on how it is going, gets a verdict in every season review, and is graded on the Manager Legacy screen when the career ends. It has no effect on matches.
handbook.a39: A youth intake arrives every season. Your academy coach and the Centre of Excellence both raise the quality of what comes through, and the better your setup the more likely a genuine prospect appears. You get an honest preview before intake day and a graded report afterwards. Development deals run out at 21: promote a lad to a professional contract from his player page before the summer he turns 21, or he leaves as a free agent. You are warned a full season ahead.
handbook.a4: The Game Plan tab has two halves: With the Ball is the four attacking sliders, Without the Ball is how your fifteen defend. Line Speed trades aggression for discipline: a blitz makes more tackles and more turnovers but gives away more penalties and cards, a drift stays clean and gives them room. Width is a match-up, read at kick-off: a wide defensive line smothers an expansive attack, but a tight pick-and-go side runs straight through the middle of it, and a narrow line does the reverse. Both dials start in the middle, where they cost and gain nothing. Every opposition coach sets them too (a Blitz Defence coach flies off the line, a Counter-Punch side sits back and soaks), and the briefing card shows the opponent's defensive shape so your attack can answer it.
handbook.a40: Yes, but only when something weakens its hand, and the player page tells you what that is before you bid. The strongest card you can hold is a contract running out in the summer, because they would otherwise lose him for nothing. After that: a man who has barely played, one who is unhappy, a club sitting in the red, a squad already well stocked in his position, or a player the wrong side of 33. Those stack, up to about a third off in the worst case for the seller. A wanted man who is playing every week at a solvent club will not move a penny, and the screen says so rather than letting you waste a window finding out.
handbook.a41: Two stages. First the fee: the stepper starts at the asking price and you move up or down from there, and a low bid can be refused outright. Then personal terms: weekly wage, a signing-on fee, and perks. His camp will accept, counter or walk. A promise of first-team rugby softens the wage he will take, and it is a real promise that gets remembered.
handbook.a42: Your wage budget is a weekly ceiling on what the squad can cost. Two players can be named marquee, and their wages sit outside that ceiling, which is how you keep one star you could not otherwise afford. Everyone else counts.
handbook.a43: Three ways. Set a focus league and your scout builds knowledge there over time. Watch the Scouting Agency boards for players the world is talking about. Or commission a specific search from the Shortlist tab: a three, six or nine-month brief for a named position. The longer the brief and the better the scout, the better the name that comes back, and the written report grades what the scout found.
handbook.a44: Because you do not know him yet. Scouting knowledge runs 0 to 100 and rises as your scouts watch him. Below a certain point his potential is a range, not a number. Your own players are fully known from day one.
handbook.a45: A player in the final season of his deal can be signed on a free to join you next summer. He sees the season out at his club, who find out from the press release. It is the cheapest way to improve a squad and everyone else is doing it too.
handbook.a46: Two. The summer window runs from the end of the league season to the start of October, and the January window covers the four weeks of January. Deadline week is flagged on Home, bids start lapsing, and late bargains turn up. The Deals tab in the Transfer Centre shows everything you have on the go. Medical jokers can be signed outside the windows.
handbook.a47: A player who is performing above his contract will have his camp come knocking. You can meet the demand, haggle a figure of your own, or refuse. Refusing a star has consequences, and so does paying every time.
handbook.a48: Yes, and you should for young players who are not going to get minutes. A postcard arrives from the club he is with telling you how he is doing. Players you take on loan belong to your current job: take a new one and they go home. A player will drop one division for game time but rarely two, so a National League club borrows from the Championship, and only the odd hungry youngster drops all the way from a top flight.
handbook.a49: Yes. On his profile, The Office card lets you praise his form or have a quiet word: two conversations a week across the squad, one per man. His personality decides how it lands: a professional answers a warning with work, a mercenary shrugs, and praising a struggling hothead reads as sarcasm. Warning a man who is playing well insults him, and the dressing room hears about it.
handbook.a5: Yes, and Physicality is the dial he decides. Pushing it up buys breakdown power and costs you yellow cards and kickable penalties, and the penalty price scales with the man in the middle. Measured over eight seasons: in front of a referee who lets a lot go at the tackle, going physical is worth about two and a half points a match to you; in front of one who is fussy there, it costs you about a point and a half. Getting that read right is worth roughly four points a match, which is more than any other single slider is worth on its own. The referee and his interpretations are named on the pre-match briefing before you pick, so the information is always there. Left in the middle the dial costs and buys nothing.
handbook.a50: Twice a season, at the start of each window, the scouting department puts up to three names on the board: aimed at your thinnest positions and ageing shirts, and every one inside your budget and wage room. The names come from your scouts' own view of the market, so a better-run department proposes better players. Tap a name in the memo to open his profile and bid.
handbook.a51: A 0 to 100 reading of how safe your job is. Results move it most, then the objectives you were set, then how you handle the press and whether you keep your promises. It appears on the Home dashboard, and a half-term report card spells out where you stand. Let it fall far enough and you will be sacked. The board's patience depends on the club. At a title favourite it reacts hard to every swing, so a season off the pace is a real crisis, and if you leave things alone you can be out of a job by the spring. At a club with modest ambitions it barely reacts to a mid-table finish, because nobody expected more.
handbook.a52: In: a weekly commercial and broadcast share set by the club's reputation, gate receipts from home matches, club shop takings, prize money at the end of the season, and transfer fees. Out: player wages, backroom wages, upkeep on the ground and the estate, and whatever you spend. The Finances screen lists every line.
handbook.a53: What it costs to open the doors, every week of the year, match or no match. The ground has to be heated, mown, stewarded and insured, and every facility level is a building with staff inside it. That is why an upgrade is a commitment: a better gym is a bill that keeps coming. The figure is on the Finances screen.
handbook.a54: There are nine facilities and each runs from level 0 to level 5. You cannot buy them: you ask the board on the Club Infrastructure page, and the board weighs the price against the reserves and its confidence in you. Confidence also decides how much the board pays: on 78 or more it covers 70 per cent of the bill, on 70 or more 55 per cent, on 58 or more about a third, and below that nothing. Below 45 the answer is no whatever the balance says. Approved work takes three weeks for the first level and twelve for the last, and a new stand takes six to sixteen weeks depending on its size. Only one project runs at a time, and after a refusal you wait two months before you can ask again.
handbook.a55: Training Pitch: a true surface sharpens the breakdown and the handling in every match, and the squad develops faster on it; a bog blunts both and hurts people in training. Gym: condition recovered every week. Recovery Centre: shorter layoffs. Training Paddock: attribute training bites more often. Kicking Enclosure: sharper goal kicking. Briefing Suite: match preparation and the analyst both land harder. Centre of Excellence: better academy intakes. Club Shop: retail income every week, more when the fans are happy. Hospitality and Boxes: every home gate is worth 4 per cent more per level. Each card on the Infrastructure page states its current effect in plain numbers.
handbook.a56: Usually one of three reasons, and it says which. Not enough of the season played to judge demand, a ground that is not full enough as it is, or reserves that will not carry the build. There is a fourth: every club has a catchment, and once the ground holds about everyone who would come, more seats would be empty seats. The Infrastructure page states your catchment so you can see where the ceiling is.
handbook.a57: It did not take it, it spent it. A board will not let a large surplus sit in a deposit account while the club stands still, so over the summer anything well beyond a season of wages plus a float goes back into the club: a build on the estate, the ground debt, the academy, the community programme. The news item says what it went on, and the terraces notice.
handbook.a58: Yes. Fan mood runs from mutinous to bouncing and shows on the Home dashboard. A happy crowd turns up in bigger numbers, lifts the side at home, and buys more in the shop. Results move it, and so do signings, sales and the things you say in press conferences.
handbook.a59: Derbies are fixed by geography and history. Grudges you earn: a bad-tempered match, a poached player, a public dig. Both make the next meeting spicier, with more cards, a hostile crowd and a form book that means nothing. The club screen keeps the ledger.
handbook.a6: No, and it used to be. Winding Kicking up gives your kicking unit more of the game and pins them in their half, which is exactly what you want in wind and rain. It also means you carry less: your attack and your breakdown both drop for it. Across a season the two roughly cancel, so it is a read on the weather, the opposition and your own boot rather than a setting to leave at one end. If you have a siege gun at ten and a shaky pack, kick. If your strength is width and offloads, do not.
handbook.a60: Questions arrive before and after matches and you choose the tone of your answer. Confidence lifts your squad and needles the opposition, who will remember it. Caution keeps everyone calm. Promises made here are recorded, and broken ones cost you.
handbook.a61: New owners can arrive at your club. It usually means a war chest, a honeymoon period and new expectations. Sometimes it means none of that, and the club has simply been sold to someone with less money.
handbook.a62: You have three things to sell: the front of the shirt, the naming rights to the ground, and the kit supply. Each is a contract with a value and a length, and the Commercial tab on the Finances screen is where you sign them. A long deal pays under the going rate because the sponsor is buying certainty off you. A short one pays over the odds and puts you back in the market sooner, which is where a good season is worth real money. Some offers carry a performance clause and start below market: deliver it and it is the best deal in the building, miss it and you have sold cheap.
handbook.a63: Deals run out. When one does you are told, and until you sign somebody that slot pays nothing at all, which is a real hole in a weekly budget. The three you inherit are staggered so they do not all fall due in the same summer, but they do fall due.
handbook.a64: Boxes and lounges make every home crowd worth more at the gate, four per cent per level. They also cost more to run than any other building on the estate, because a box needs chefs and hosts whether or not there is a match. Break-even is an average home crowd of about nine thousand across a season of roughly fourteen home gates, so at a full Premier Division ground a level returns about one and a half times its upkeep, and more again at a big one. Below that it is a straight loss. Expanding the ground adds seats; this makes the seats you have worth more.
handbook.a65: Every six weeks the league looks at what every club actually did across that window, counting league, cup and European matches alike. To be in the running at all a manager needs three matches and two wins from them, so a single good afternoon wins nothing. Beyond the bar it is merit: beating a better side counts for more than beating a worse one, winning away counts for more than winning at home, and the size of the win matters. If nobody in the league did enough, the award is not given that month.
handbook.a66: Build a reputation, then apply from the Job Centre when a vacancy that suits you appears. Your chances depend on your reputation against the club's standing. If you are doing well somewhere, bigger clubs will come to you: a tap on the shoulder arrives in your inbox, and it does not stay open long. And if you are out of work, modest clubs will give you a second chance: experience counts for more the further down you look, so the way back in is usually a rung or two below the job you left.
handbook.a67: It does. A public loyalty vow is recorded, and if you walk out within a few weeks of making one, every paper runs the clip. Your new board notes how cheaply the last promise was sold, and the away end has a song ready for your return.
handbook.a68: Your name, your record, your trophies and your badges. Not much else. The facilities belong to the club, so you inherit whatever the new one has. The backroom staff there are the backroom staff there. Grudges, the head-to-head book, the decisions ledger and the ground record all start blank, because they belong to the old place.
handbook.a69: A running list on your Profile of the choices that mattered: appointments, board requests, briefs, analyst reads you followed, expansions. Each is marked as having worked out or not. It is there so a long career has a story you can read back rather than a number.
handbook.a7: You do. When your side wins a penalty in range, the game stops and asks: posts, corner, or tap and go. Your kicker's goal kicking and the angle both matter, and so does the scoreboard. Taking three when you need seven is how games get lost.
handbook.a70: Because the room outranks you. The game compares your reputation to the standing of the 23 you pick: walk into a star dressing room as an unproven name and the squad questions every instruction. Patterns are drilled at up to half pace, team talks land with a fraction of their weight, and a fine handed out by a manager without a record can turn into a stand-off. The Manager Profile shows where you stand. The way out is the same as in real life: win. Trust earned through results cancels the strain completely, because a room that believes in you stops caring about your CV, and a trophy settles it for good.
handbook.a71: Yes, if one asks. The unions watch managers with a reputation of 64 or better and can call twice a season, the smaller nations first; the biggest only come for names in the mid-80s. Accept from your Manager Profile and you run the country alongside the club. The Club & Country screen has everything: the ranking, the union's confidence, your Test record and the squad for the window. When camp is open you can drop a name and call up the next man: any qualified player in the game, any age, any rating, only the injured refused. The union sets a maximum squad size and will not let it drop below 23. On a Test weekend your assistant takes any club match while you take the country. Leave the job and your Test record stays on your Manager Profile. You can step down from either job on the same screen. A World Championship is the biggest thing in the game. The Job Centre shows how close your reputation is.
handbook.a72: Every four years. The men's is in 2027, 2031 and on, with twenty nations in four pools of five; the women's is in 2029, 2033 and on, with sixteen nations in four pools of four. Pools are seeded from the live world rankings, so four years of Test results decide who gets the kind pool and who gets the group of death. Then quarter-finals, semis and a final. It runs in the opening weeks of the season and your internationals are away until it is decided, so plan the early club rounds around the gaps. The usual autumn Tests make way for it that year. Hold a national job when one comes round and you coach every match of it: your seeding sets the bar, the union marks you against it, and the review lands either way. A World Championship won stays on a player's honours for good, and on yours.
handbook.a73: In England the trapdoor is a match: the Premier Division's bottom club hosts the Championship winner in a one-off play-off after the finals, and the winner plays top-flight rugby next season. Everywhere else it is automatic: bottom of the top flight down, champion of the second tier up. European places come from final league standings: the top five of the Premier Division, six of the Elite 14 and five of the UPC make the Continental Cup, and the next band down from each goes into the Continental Shield.
handbook.a74: Three places. Manager Profile has your badges, specialities and trophy cabinet. Manager Legacy has the milestones. The Annals hold every season you have managed, one row each, and the Roll of Honour holds the world's: champions, Players of the Year, and the Hall of Fame.
handbook.a75: The game saves itself every week, so you cannot lose a season to a closed tab. Game Status has four slots for manual backups or parallel careers, a Send a copy button that hands the save to your phone's share sheet, and an Export Career button that writes it to a file. It all lives in this browser's storage, which is why those two matter: clearing your browsing data takes the career with it, and on an iPhone Safari clears the storage of sites it has not seen for a week or so unless the game is on your home screen.
handbook.a76: The dark theme. Switch it with the button next to Continue, or in Settings. It is made for reading a phone at night, and every screen works in it.
handbook.a77: Six: English, French, Spanish, Italian, Japanese and Afrikaans. Pick one at the foot of the title screen, before a career even exists, or change it any time in Settings. It changes everything the game says to you, including the assistant's game plan, the coach's verdict and the analyst's read, which are written fresh each time you look. Match commentary and inbox stories stay in the language they were written in: they are filed into the career as they happen, and a report that changed its words between two readings would not be a record of anything.
handbook.a78: Two ways, on the Save / Load screen. Send a copy hands the save file to your phone's share sheet, so it goes to a cloud drive, a chat with yourself or an email in two taps. That is the one that matters, because a file in Downloads is on the same phone as the career it is backing up. Export Career saves the file to the device instead, which is what you want on a computer. Either file goes back in through Import on any device. The game reminds you once a season, because storage clearing itself is the only way this game can lose a career.
handbook.a79: The game itself collects nothing: no account, no sign-in, no analytics, and no network request at all once it has loaded (the build fails automatically if anyone adds one). Everything is saved on your device. The web version has no adverts and no store. App store versions come inside an app that can show adverts and sell optional extras; the adverts and payments are handled by that app and the store, not by the game, and your advert privacy choices are in Settings. Pro Manager removes the adverts and changes nothing about the rugby. Other items, such as board funding or lifting the salary cap, do change your save. None of them plays a match for you.
handbook.catWordsSub: the terms the game uses, in plain English
handbook.a80: The ball has gone out of play, so it is thrown back in down a corridor of forwards who lift a jumper to catch it. Win your own throw and you keep possession; steal theirs and you have the ball deep in their half.
handbook.a81: Eight forwards from each side bind together and push for a ball fed into the middle. It restarts play after a minor mistake, and a dominant pack wins penalties from it as well as possession.
handbook.a82: A tackled player puts the ball down and players from both sides bind over it, on their feet, trying to win it back. Nobody may use hands once it forms, which is why the fight for it is with feet and shoulders.
handbook.a83: The same contest as a ruck, but the ball carrier is still on his feet and players bind on to him. A strong pack drives it forward, which is how a lot of tries are scored from close range.
handbook.a84: The few seconds after a tackle, when possession is genuinely up for grabs. Most matches are decided here rather than in open play, which is why breakdown work is one of the things your forwards are rated on.
handbook.a85: A player who gets over a tackled opponent and grabs the ball before a ruck forms. Do it legally and you win a penalty; get it fractionally wrong and you give one away, which is why jackals are prized and risky.
handbook.a86: Possession changing hands during play rather than at a set piece. Turnovers are the cheapest tries in rugby, because the defence is usually out of position the moment one happens.
handbook.a87: Losing the ball forwards off the hands or arms. Play stops and the other side get the put-in at a scrum.
handbook.a88: A pass made in the tackle, before going to ground. It keeps the move alive and skips the ruck altogether. It is the quickest way through a set defence, and the easiest way to lose the ball.
handbook.a89: A try is five points and earns a conversion kick worth two more. A penalty kick at goal is three. A drop goal, kicked out of hand in open play, is also three.
handbook.a90: The line 22 metres out from each try line. It matters for kicking: inside your own 22 you may kick straight into touch and keep the ground you gained, outside it you may not.
handbook.q91: Why kick to the corner instead of at the posts?
handbook.a91: Three points from the tee are near certain; the corner gives you a lineout five metres out and a chance at seven. Take the points when three is enough, take the corner when it is not.
handbook.a92: A short, high kick from the scrum-half, usually out of a ruck, meant to be chased and contested in the air. It is how a side escapes its own half without handing over easy possession.
handbook.q93: What is an up-and-under, or a grubber?
handbook.a93: An up-and-under is a high kick that hangs long enough for chasers to arrive under it. A grubber is kicked along the ground through a defence, for a chaser to gather behind them.
handbook.a94: Kick from inside your own half and put it into touch inside their 22, and you throw into the lineout instead of them. It rewards an accurate kick and drags defenders back to cover the space behind.
handbook.a95: A scrum or a lineout: play restarting from a fixed, organised position rather than a scramble. A side with a reliable set piece controls when the game speeds up, which is what your tight five are paid for.
handbook.q96: What is the gain line, and what is a phase?
handbook.a96: The gain line is the imaginary line across the pitch where the last ruck was - crossing it means you actually moved forward. A phase is one carry and the ruck that follows it, so 'six phases' means six carries with no whistle.
handbook.q97: Who are the front row, the tight five and the back row?
handbook.a97: The front row is two props and a hooker, the men who meet first in a scrum. Add the two locks and it is the tight five, the pushing engine. The back row, two flankers and a number 8, are the forwards who cover the most ground.
handbook.q98: What do the scrum-half and fly-half do?
handbook.a98: The scrum-half feeds the ball out of every ruck and scrum, so he touches it more than anyone on the pitch. The fly-half decides what happens next: pass, kick or run. Usually the goal kicker too.
handbook.a99: The two wings and the full-back: the last line of defence and usually the quickest men in the side. They field kicks, chase them, and finish most of the tries.
handbook.q100: What is a 'bomb squad', or a 6-2 split?
handbook.a100: How you divide the eight replacements. A 6-2 split is six forwards and two backs, so you can change your whole pack late and out-muscle a tiring team. It leaves you thin if a back gets injured.
handbook.a101: The Television Match Official, who checks a try or foul play on replay. In this game about one try in six goes upstairs, and roughly a third of those are chalked off. A try with a forward pass in the build-up always goes to the TMO: nine in ten are ruled out, and the rest stand as tight calls.
handbook.q102: What are yellow and red cards, and the sin bin?
handbook.a102: A yellow card sends a player to the sin bin for ten minutes and you play a man short. A red card removes him for the rest of the match. Both cost far more than the penalty that caused them.
handbook.a104: A short-term signing to cover a long injury. When a player is out for six weeks or more, the Medical Centre lets you sign one free agent who plays that position. The wage sits outside the salary cap while the cover lasts, though the club still pays it every week, and the deal ends when the injured player is fit, leaves the club, or the season ends. One joker per injured player.
handbook.q105: Can an injured player play through it?
handbook.a105: In the last three weeks of a layoff, yes, from the Medical Centre. The injury becomes a knock: available to pick, but starting each match short of full energy, and every match played on it risks a flare-up and a longer layoff. The button states the risk: 20% a match sent back a week early, 46% three weeks early. Rest instead puts the layoff back as it was. A head injury is never played through.
handbook.q106: Does a big crowd sway the referee?
handbook.a106: On a big day it can. In front of a large home crowd, in a derby or in a knockout, the tight calls lean towards the home side, and the pre-match briefing says so when they will. It is the crowd, not the referee: the same match in front of empty stands would not lean.
handbook.q107: When does the pitch come on during a match?
handbook.a107: For the moments that matter. In between, the match is the commentary with the live stats underneath. Highlights in Match Settings (the cog on the match screen) chooses which moments: Key shows tries and tries sent to the TMO; Extended adds kicks at goal and breaks into the 22. A highlight plays the phases that led to it, then the finish, and the commentary keeps pace with the picture. In the last ten minutes of a close match (seven points or fewer in it), Key shows the kicks and the attacks too.
handbook.q108: Is a match I watch different from one I skip or play with Instant Result?
handbook.a108: No. Every match in the game, yours or anybody else's, watched line by line, skipped or played with Instant Result, runs on the same engine with the same rules. Watching only decides what is written down for you to read. When the other dugout changes its plan to counter you, the commentary says so.
handbook.a103: A Head Injury Assessment. A player who takes a blow to the head leaves the field to be checked; he returns only if he passes, and the game will not let him back if he does not.
handbook.a8: The week's training focus, set on the Tactics screen before the game. Attack, defence, set piece, fitness or recovery. It gives a small edge in that area for the coming match, and the Analysis and Briefing Suite makes the edge bigger. Recovery buys back condition instead, which is what you want on a short turnaround.
handbook.a9: Before each match he names the unit he thinks the opposition is weakest in. If he is right you get a small edge there, and you can turn his read straight into that week's preparation with one tap. He is not always right. His accuracy climbs with the Briefing Suite and with a better assistant, and the Prep page keeps his record so you can decide how much to trust him.
